name: ASA (Acrylonitrile Styrene Acrylate)
chemical_makeup: Acrylonitrile styrene acrylate — a styrenic terpolymer in which a grafted acrylate-ester rubber phase is dispersed in a styrene-acrylonitrile (SAN) matrix. The saturated acrylate rubber replaces ABS's polybutadiene, removing the double bonds UV attacks; amorphous engineering thermoplastic
summary: ABS reformulated for sunlight: the same styrenic stiffness, impact resistance and ~100 °C glass transition, but with a weather-stable acrylate rubber phase that makes it the best UV and outdoor performer among common filaments. The cost is ABS-grade warping that demands an enclosure, and high styrene-dominated emissions that demand ventilation.

printing.notes: Brand starting points differ: Polymaker 240-280 °C (start 250), Prusament 260±10 °C, Bambu 240-270 °C. Bed 90-110 °C (Polymaker), 110±5 °C (Prusament), 80-100 °C with glue (Bambu). Keep part cooling low — heavy cooling splits layers. An enclosed, draft-free ~60 °C chamber is the ideal; a passive enclosure suffices for small parts, while large flat parts effectively require active chamber heat. Modern enclosed CoreXY machines run 200-250 mm/s; legacy/Bowden setups sit at 35-70 mm/s. Hardened nozzle only for CF/GF-filled ASA.

feeding.notes: Listed AMS-compatible by Bambu and feeds like ABS — rigid, non-abrasive in unfilled form, moderate hygroscopy. CF/GF-filled ASA is the exception, as with every abrasive filament in an AMS. Enclosure: ASA needs the retained chamber heat even more than ABS does, so enclosure_open_for_cooling is false; Bambu and QIDI both specify the cover installed.

drying.dryness_validation: No popping or crackling while extruding; no bubbles or voids in a hand-pulled test strand; consistent glossy extrudate; no increase in stringing on a retraction test
drying.notes: Bambu's drying wiki gives 75-85 °C for 8 h (oven) or 90-100 °C for 12 h (heated-bed method); Bambu's own ASA product page states 80 °C for 8 h. ASA does not need the routine drying nylon does, but it absorbs enough to matter after open-air storage.

storage.recommendations: Store sealed with desiccant, targeting under 20% RH. Absorbs less aggressively than nylon or PETG but noticeably more than PLA, so resealing between prints is worthwhile rather than optional.

price.notes: 2025-2026 pricing for standard unfilled grades: budget brands ~$18-22, Bambu $29.99/kg, premium Prusament/Polymaker and specialty colours ~$35-45 per kg. Exact bounds unverified.

recommended: automotive exterior trim and license-plate frames
mailboxes and other permanently sun-exposed housings
drone and RC frames exposed to sun
not_recommended: indoor decor where PLA would do the job more easily
printing in unenclosed, unventilated occupied rooms (styrene VOCs)
tight-tolerance small parts printed without an enclosure (corner lift and warp)
flexible or energy-absorbing applications needing elastomer behaviour

properties.notes: Density spans 1.05 (Bambu) to 1.08-1.09 (Polymaker/partmfg.com) with Prusament at 1.07 — 1.07 recorded. HDT from the Prusament TDS is 93 °C at 0.45 MPa and 86 °C at 1.8 MPa; Bambu cites 100 °C without stating a load. Tensile strength shows a notable brand spread: Bambu 37±3 MPa, Prusament 42-45 MPa, Polymaker/partmfg.com 47.1 MPa. Shrinkage and max service temperature are typical-for-styrenics estimates rather than datasheet values. CNC Kitchen measured a bending modulus of ~2300 MPa for ASA against ~3300 MPa for PLA, and ~30% impact energy absorbed versus 8% for PLA and 14% for PETG. 3D-Fuel's Pro ASA sheet (technical library, read 2026-08-01, branded 'Workday ASA') adds NOTHING to this block: it is a one-page marketing-and-print-settings sheet with no density, tensile, flexural, impact, HDT, Tg, shrinkage or melt-flow figure and no ASTM/ISO method cited anywhere — the only ASA document in 3D-Fuel's library and the weakest of the seven. Its sole quantitative content is 230-260 °C nozzle and 110 °C bed. Snapmaker's ASA product page (owner-provided link, read 2026-08-06) is the fourth branded ASA sheet here and the most complete of them, and the only one publishing Z-axis figures: tensile 43.8 ± 0.8 MPa XY against 32 ± 1.8 MPa Z, bending 73.4 ± 2.1 MPa at a 3206 ± 108 MPa modulus XY, notched impact 10.3 ± 0.4 kJ/m² XY against 6.7 ± 1.4 kJ/m² Z, Tg 98 °C at 10 °C/min, HDT 103 °C at 0.45 MPa, Vicat 105 °C, water absorption 0.4 %, density 1.13 g/cm³ at 23 °C. Its tensile figure lands inside the recorded 37-47 MPa band and effectively on Prusament's 42-45 MPa, which is the strongest independent support the mid-range value has had. Its density does not fit: 1.13 is above every other source. Its bending modulus of 3206 MPa is roughly 40 % above the ~2300 MPa CNC Kitchen measured on Prusament ASA, so the stiffness gap to PLA that entry describes is formulation-dependent rather than a property of ASA as a class. Print settings 240-280 °C nozzle (exactly the recorded range), 75-100 °C bed, 50-200 mm/s, fan off, pre-dry 70 °C for 7 h. No ASTM/ISO method and no diameter tolerance are stated.

compatibility.notes: Welds chemically to ABS — same SAN matrix family — which makes ABS/ASA the standard multi-material pairing for outdoor parts. The PETG joint is weaker and order-dependent: PETG printed first with ASA on top is stronger than the reverse, so treat it as semi-compatible rather than a true weld. No chemical bond to PLA, PC, PA, PP, TPU or TPE (mechanical interlock only; specifics unverified). PVA and BVOH are unusable as supports because they degrade below ASA's 240-280 °C nozzle window. HIPS is the conventional breakaway/limonene-soluble support for the ABS/ASA family, though the documentation is for ABS and only inferred for ASA.

plate_recommendations.notes: Works at 90-110 °C bed. ASA still lifts at the corners on larger footprints, so a glue stick or dedicated adhesion promoter (Magigoo-type) is commonly applied even on textured PEI, and brims help. Bambu's 80-100 °C bed guidance explicitly assumes glue.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Prusa notes ASA adhesion on satin is somewhat lower than PLA or PETG; a brim and draft shield cover the gap.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Some vendors recommend an adhesion promoter for ASA specifically even though bare adhesion is generally adequate.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): ASA can over-adhere to smooth PEI much like PETG; a separator prevents film damage on big footprints.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Same as ABS. On a rigid plate a lifted corner cannot be rescued by flexing, so use a brim and an enclosure.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Same conflicting-source caveat as ABS. Use a brim on large footprints.

Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Not separately named by BuildTak (unverified), but chemically and thermally close enough to ABS that it behaves the same in practice — near the top of the sheet's rated bed range,
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): As ABS; the bed temperature also runs near the practical ceiling of a PP-based coating.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): As ABS; the required bed temperature alone puts it outside the coating's intended range.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Same as ABS — the required 90-110 C bed exceeds what the PC sheet tolerates without surface damage.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): As ABS — thermal and adhesion envelope both exceeded in practice.

emissions.notes: Grouped with ABS and ULTRAT as the top VOC emitters among common filaments (irrgang.dev, citing an academic emissions study), dominated by styrene. Ultrafine particle emission is elevated and comparable to ABS. Print in an enclosure vented externally, or filtered through HEPA plus activated carbon; do not run ASA in an occupied unventilated room.

safety_notes: Styrene is a respiratory irritant and a suspected carcinogen on chronic exposure — the enclosure is a containment measure as much as a warp-control one. Carbon- and glass-filled ASA grades are abrasive and need a hardened nozzle; do not inhale fibre dust when sanding them.
additional_notes: Z-strength is the weak axis and is strongly process-dependent: CNC Kitchen measured Z at only ~29% of XY strength when printed unenclosed, against ~46-55% for PLA and PETG, with an enclosure recovering roughly 20%. Orient loads in-plane and treat the enclosure as a structural requirement, not a cosmetic one.

provenance.conflicts: HDT: Prusament measures 93 °C at 0.45 MPa and 86 °C at 1.8 MPa while Bambu cites 100 °C without specifying the load basis — 93 °C recorded on the schema's 0.45 MPa basis. Density: Bambu 1.05, Prusament 1.07, Polymaker/partmfg.com 1.08-1.09. Tensile strength spans 37±3 MPa (Bambu) to 47.1 MPa (Polymaker/partmfg.com), a spread too wide to be measurement noise alone. Drying: Bambu's wiki says 75-85 °C while Bambu's own ASA product page says 80 °C. Shrinkage (~0.4-0.7%), max continuous service temperature (~80-90 °C) and the 'moderate' hygroscopy class are typical-for-class or community estimates, not datasheet figures. HIPS as an ASA support is documented for ABS and inferred for ASA. 2026-08-01 update (3D-Fuel technical library published — owner-provided link): 3D-Fuel's Pro ASA document was checked and contains NO mechanical or thermal data at all — no density, tensile, HDT, Tg or shrinkage, and no test methods — so it neither confirms nor contradicts anything here and no value changed. It is the only sheet in the library with no SDS counterpart and the only one carrying no test data, which is itself worth recording: the wide brand spreads in this entry (density 1.05-1.09, tensile 37-47 MPa, HDT 93-100 °C) get no help from a third manufacturer. Its 230 °C nozzle minimum is 10 °C below the recorded 240 °C floor and its 110 °C bed sits at the top of the recorded range, both consistent with Prusament's guidance. 2026-08-06 update (Snapmaker ASA launch — owner-provided link): NO recorded value changed. Confirmations: the 240-280 °C nozzle range matches the recorded range exactly, the first source to do so; tensile 43.8 ± 0.8 MPa XY sits essentially on the recorded 43 MPa recommendation; the 75-100 °C bed overlaps Bambu's 80-100 °C; enclosure-required matches enclosure_recommended true with no heated chamber demanded. Contradictions: density 1.13 g/cm³ is above every other source — Bambu 1.05, Prusament 1.07, Polymaker/partmfg 1.08-1.09 — widening the spread from 1.05-1.09 to 1.05-1.13. It is a single-vendor outlier on an already-disputed field with no test method cited, so the recorded 1.07 is retained rather than re-centred, and this remains the entry's least settled number. HDT 103 °C at 0.45 MPa is 10 °C above Prusament's 93 °C on the SAME stated load basis and 3 °C above Bambu's load-unspecified 100 °C, so the HDT disagreement is now three-way with Prusament the low outlier; 93 °C is retained only because Prusament is still the sole figure backed by a published TDS with both load points. Tg 98 °C against the recorded 100 °C is within noise. Cooling fan: Snapmaker specifies OFF against the recorded 10-25 % band — but Snapmaker specifies fan-off for its ABS too, so this reads as a house rule for styrenics rather than an ASA-specific measurement, and the low-but-nonzero recorded band is kept. Drying 70 °C for 7 h is 5 °C below the recorded 75 °C floor and its time falls inside the recorded 8-12 h window's lower edge; the recorded window spans two vendors and is retained. Bed floor 75 °C is 5 °C below the recorded 80 °C minimum. Shrinkage, max service temperature and part-cooling remain unsupported by this source, which publishes none of them.

alternatives.reason: The cheaper indoor equivalent at the same strength and heat class, with better compression (7 vs 6), better layer adhesion (5 vs 4) and acetone vapour smoothing — but it yellows and embrittles in sunlight (uv 2 vs 9, weather 2 vs 9), so indoor only.

Cures ASA's defining warp with glass fiber (warp 5 vs 7, dim 8 vs 7, HDT 97-99 °C vs 93 °C) while keeping the full UV package, at $34-45 vs $18-45, a mandatory hardened nozzle, a worse layer bond (3 vs 4) and no AMS feeding.
The stiff outdoor grade: compression 8 vs 6 and warp 4 vs 7 with UV unchanged, but the layer bond degrades further (adhesion 3 vs 4) and price jumps to $70-112 from $18-45.

If the outdoor part is low-stress and low-heat, PETG prints far easier with no enclosure (ease 7 vs 5, warp 3 vs 7) and bonds far better (adhesion 9 vs 4) at the same money — with a much shorter UV life (uv 5 vs 9) and less heat (temp 5 vs 7).
